title: Chapter 184 – The Seven Arrive
html:
[The Garden Infirmary and the Dock – Bell]

Bell is elbow-deep in a farmer's abdomen when the bell rings, and she does not stop sewing until the last knot is tied.

It is the third hour of the evening, the ninth day since the tide, and the infirmary is still full. Forty-one cots. Sixty-three, if you count the pallets on the floor between them. The wounded lie in rows under the long windows, in the yellow light of a hundred lamps, and the air is thick with the smell of clove and boiled linen and the sour sweetness of infection. Bell has been in this room, by her own count, for eleven days out of fourteen. She has stopped noticing the smell. She has stopped noticing her hands.

"There," she says, and snips the thread. "Keep him warm. If the belly swells, call me."

The apprentice nods. He is nineteen, sallow, hollow-eyed, and he has done everything she has asked for nine days without a word of complaint. She pats his arm, and straightens, and stretches until her spine cracks.

The bell rings again.

It is not the Hall bell. It is lower, deeper, a single plain peal that she feels in her sternum before she hears it. A pause. Then another. Seven strokes, evenly spaced, rolling up the stair from the bottom of the world.

Seven.

She stands very still with the needle in her hand.

"Mistress Bell?" says the apprentice. "Is that...?"

"It's the Dock." She wipes her hands on her apron. "Someone is at the Gate."

"Another attack?"

"No." She is already unfastening the apron. "That is a welcome."

* * *

She meets Tian Mo at the head of the stair, and he looks like a man who has seen his own ghost.

He is standing in the lamp-bright corridor with his pinned sleeve and his plain staff, flanked by six guards in the quilted gowns of the fifth landing, and none of them are speaking. Dai has her spear ground on the flagstones as if she means to drive it through the floor. The younger guards are pale. And at the rail, leaning over the dark with a hand pressed to his chest, stands Lin Jian, thin as a rake, in a blanket, staring down the seven hundred and one steps with an expression Bell has never seen on him.

"Jian," she says sharply. "You should be in bed."

"I felt it."

"Felt what?"

"The door." His voice is very quiet. "Mei opened it. Just a crack. I heard it from the kitchen." He does not turn his head. "They're coming up."

"Who?"

"My brothers."

Bell's mouth opens. Shuts.

He means the seven. She knows that. She has heard Jian speak of them, in the nights at the infirmary, when the cough kept him from sleeping and he lay on his side talking in a low voice to the ceiling. The seven. The children in the Hall. They are the same as me, Bell. The same work. The same hand. She has not understood it. She has nodded, and held his wrist, and counted his pulse. Eight Operators, he told her once. Eight working copies of one man's mind, laid down in eight newborns by a Gate that wanted a keeper. Seven asleep in a hall. One awake in a garden.

And now they're coming home, she thinks.

"Tian Mo," she says. "How many steps?"

"Seven hundred and one."

"And how long will they take?"

"The youngest is five. The oldest is nineteen. They've been asleep for..." He gives up. "I don't know. Hours."

"Then send for a litter. And hot water. And Qinghe's soup, if she can spare it." She rolls her sleeves. "I'll be at the foot of the stair."

* * *

They are not what she expects.

She reaches the Dock at midnight, breathless, with a satchel on her shoulder and an apprentice running at her heels, and stops dead at the cavern's mouth. She has been bracing for the worst. She has pictured seven pale shapes carried out on boards, limp and wasted and trailing tubes, like the sleepers in the stories. She has pictured a nurse's cart. She has pictured a long night of fighting for their breath.

What she sees instead is a child running.

He tears across the polished black floor of the Dock in his bare feet at full tilt, a small boy of five in a white gown too big for him, with a mop of dark hair and a gap in his front teeth. He is shrieking with laughter. He circles the iron scaffold of the great bell twice, ducks beneath Dai's spear, narrowly misses a startled guard, and skids to a halt in front of Bell with his arms thrown wide.

"Hello!" he says. "Are you the healer?"

"I—yes."

"I'm Tao." He grins. "I'm number seven. The others said I couldn't run, but I can! I ran all the way down! Look!" He hops on one leg. "Did you see? Do you have a cat?"

Bell stares at him.

"Tao!" A girl's voice, sharp, resigned. "Come back here. You're being rude."

"She's the healer, Cheng, she said so."

"That isn't a reason to shout at her."

The speaker comes forward from the shadow of the Gate wall, and Bell's breath catches. She is nineteen, tall, thin-faced, with spectacles pushed up into a heavy braid of black hair and a scholar's stoop to her shoulders. She wears the same white gown as the child, belted at the waist with a length of cord. Her feet are bare. And in her arms, wrapped in a quilt, is a little boy of three with a rabbit.

It is a real rabbit. It sits in the crook of his elbow, brown and twitching, with its nose wrinkling at the cold. The boy is asleep with his thumb in his mouth.

"Forgive my brother," says Cheng Hui. She inclines her head. "He's never been out of the Hall. I'm told he gets excited." A faint, wry smile. "I am Cheng Hui, of the Court. This is Ao. That is Duan Ke." She nods at the shadow. "And behind him, Hai Ren, Zhen Li, and Mo Yan. We were told we might find you here."

Bell turns.

They are standing in a line before the Gate wall, in the ring of blue lamps: five more children, in white, barefoot. A tall sullen boy of sixteen with a long pale blade strapped to his back. A solemn, round-faced boy of fourteen with his hands folded in his sleeves. A boy of eleven with a lamp in his fist, unlit. A girl of eight with dark hair cut straight across her forehead and a stick of charcoal tucked behind one ear.

And behind them, in the seam of the Gate, framed in the pale gray light of an open door, a woman in a nurse's cap stands with her hands folded.

She meets Bell's eyes across the Dock. She bows, once, deeply, without a word.

Then the seam closes, softly, and she is gone.

* * *

The climb takes five hours, and the children sing for most of it.

It is a thin high rambling song, nothing Bell recognizes, with words in no language she has heard. Zhen Li begins it. The lamp-boy walks at the head of the line with his unlit lantern held before him like a priest with an offering, humming under his breath, and one by one the others take it up. Tao skips. Ao sleeps on Cheng Hui's shoulder with the rabbit, and does not wake. Duan Ke walks apart, with a hand on his sword-hilt, glowering at the guards. Mo Yan, the little girl, walks at the rear with her charcoal in her hand and her eyes tilted up, tracing patterns in the air, as if reading a score nobody else can see.

Bell walks beside Hai Ren, and counts his pulse.

It is, she finds, a remarkable pulse. Slow. Even. Forty to the minute, deep and strong, with a long rest between beats that feels like a held breath. His skin is cool and dry. His pupils are wide. He climbs the steps with a calm, measured tread, as if the seven hundred and one were nothing more than the stairs of a house.

"You're not tired," she says.

"No, Healer."

"You've been asleep for years."

"Yes." He glances at her with grave, clear eyes. "It does not seem to matter. The Hall keeps us. We do not tire there."

"But you tire here."

"Not yet." He pauses at a landing, and looks at the roots that spill from the wall like white hair, and touches one gently. It curls round his finger. "But I think we will. The Nurse said it would take some time. Perhaps a year. Our hearts are tied to the Hall by a kind of thread. When it frays, we fade."

"Fade."

"Grow slow. Grow sleepy. Then stop." He says it without fear, as one reports the weather. "It is not painful, I am told. But I would prefer to avoid it, if possible. There is a great deal I would like to see."

She does not trust herself to answer. They climb on.

On the fourth landing, a guard lies on a pallet against the wall, in the blue gloom, with his chest bound in bloody linen. He is one of Tian Mo's. A broken-ribbed man of fifty, who was carried here three days ago and never moved on, because the healers said it was too late to risk it. He is breathing in short shallow rasps. His lips are blue. His eyes are open, and fixed on the ceiling, and full of a terror so naked that Bell has to look away.

Hai Ren stops.

"Healer," he says gently. "May I?"

"May you what?"

"Ease him."

She stiffens. She has heard what the Quiet boy does. The Great Stillness, the Settling. She has heard it spoken of in the infirmary with the same hushed horror people use for the executioner. A boy of fourteen who lays his hands on the dying, and takes the fear from them, and takes with it something of himself.

"What does it cost?" she says.

"A day. Or two. Of my own." He smiles, very slightly. "I have a good many. I was told I would not use them."

"I'd rather you didn't."

"I know." He looks at her with an unnerving gentleness. "But he is afraid, Healer. And he is going to die tonight, whatever either of us does. I would not like him to do it afraid."

Bell opens her mouth. And shuts it.

She watches the boy kneel, and lay one small hand on the guard's forehead, and the other over his heart. She watches the guard's eyes find his face. She watches the terror melt out of them like frost under a hand, and the breath ease, and the blue fade from his lips. He smiles. It is a child's smile, startled, wondering. He says a name. It is not one she knows.

He dies a quarter of an hour later, quietly, in his sleep.

Hai Ren rises. He is a little paler than before. He tucks his hands into his sleeves and walks on up the stair beside her, saying nothing, and Bell finds that her cheeks are wet and does not remember when it began.

* * *

By the time they reach the infirmary, she has stopped trying to treat them as patients.

She does it anyway. It is what she is for. She sits them on the cots in a row, under the long windows, and takes their pulses and their temperatures and the color of their eyes, while the apprentice scribbles notes. She asks questions. She presses the soles of their feet. She holds a candle to their pupils and watches the light bend.

They are, in every particular, healthy. Better than healthy. Cheng Hui's hearing is acute to a degree she would not have believed. Duan Ke's reflexes are those of a cat. Zhen Li's eyes can follow a falling mote of dust. Mo Yan, the silent one, has a pulse that flutters and rushes like a bird's, and when Bell lays a hand on her throat she feels a faint, constant vibration, as if the girl were humming to herself on a pitch below hearing.

But under all that health, she finds the thread.

It is a strange thing to find. She is a healer, not a seer. She has never felt such a thing in a living body. But in each of them, when she lays two fingers to the base of the throat and closes her eyes, she senses a fine silver tension running down through the breastbone and out into the dark, like a spider's line stretched taut between two walls. It trembles. It thins. In Ao, the three-year-old, it is nearly as fine as a hair. In Tao, the five-year-old, it is thicker but fraying. In Cheng Hui, the eldest, it is almost whole.

A year, she thinks. Perhaps less.

She sits back on her heels. The seven watch her from their cots with calm eyes.

"You see it," says Duan Ke. It is the first thing he has said. His voice is rough, unused, sullen. "The cord. You can feel it."

"Yes."

"How long?"

"I don't know." She is honest. "Less than a year for the little ones. More for the older."

"Can you cut it?"

"I can't cut what I can't see."

"Can you mend it?"

Bell looks at him. He is a long pale furious boy of sixteen, with a scowl and an old sword and eyes that hold more grief than any sixteen-year-old's should. He sits on the edge of the cot with his hands clenched on his knees, and she sees that he has been holding himself like that since the Dock. He is not angry at her. He is angry at the world, the way a man is angry at a wall he cannot move.

"No," she says. "I'm sorry."

Silence. Zhen Li lifts his unlit lamp and turns it slowly in his hands. Tao has stopped smiling. Cheng Hui takes off her spectacles and begins to polish them on her sleeve, very carefully, with a small tight movement of the jaw.

It is Ao, who has been sleeping, who speaks.

"It's all right," he says sleepily. He has woken without a sound, and he sits up in the quilt with the rabbit in his lap. "We knew. We came anyway."

* * *

Jian finds her in the corridor in the small hours, and neither of them pretends to be surprised.

She is sitting on the floor outside the infirmary with her back to the wall and her knees drawn up, as she has not done since she was a girl. He lowers himself beside her, with a grunt, and the blanket slides off one shoulder. For a while they sit in the dark and listen to the seven sleeping behind the door.

"You heard," she says.

"Most of it."

"Then you know it's less than a year."

"I know." He is staring at the opposite wall. "I am a good deal less than a year myself, Bell. I do not feel that I am in a position to complain."

"That isn't funny."

"It is a little." His mouth lifts. "Ao told me, when I met him. At the Dock. He took my hand and said, Hello, Eighth. You look tired. I did not know what to say."

"What did you say?"

"I said, I am. And he said, That's all right. We are too." He lets out a long shaking breath. "Seven of them, Bell. Seven. In the Hall, in the dark, for years. I never knew them. I read their names in a register. I never once thought they might be glad to see me."

Bell reaches over and takes his hand. It is cold and light, like a bundle of dry sticks. She holds it in both of hers.

"Whatever Qinghe does tomorrow," she says, "you know it won't be enough."

"I know."

"It might buy them a year. Two. It might buy them ten. I don't know, Jian. I'm a healer, not a god. I can't promise them anything."

"Nor can I." He turns his head. His eyes are very clear in the dark. "But I think we are going to find out whether a table is stronger than a Hall. And I would very much like to be there when we do."

He does not say how long he will be. She does not ask. They sit in the corridor, shoulder to shoulder, and the lamps burn low, and for the first time in many nights Bell lets herself lean her head against his arm.

"Thirteen weeks," she says into the sleeve.

"Thirteen and four days, now. I scanned the cauldron."

"Don't count."

"I always count." He squeezes her hand. "But I will try not to tell you the number."

* * *

Yue comes in the dark before dawn, with Lin Kuang half asleep on her arm and the cracked Pebble in a cloth against her chest, and stops in front of the cot where Mo Yan lies.

The girl is awake. She has been awake all night, Bell realizes, lying on her back with her charcoal stick held in the air, tracing patterns on the ceiling, slow looping shapes that none of the sleepers can see. She turns her head as the old woman approaches. Her eyes are dark and enormous. She holds out her hand.

Yue takes it.

There is a pause. Then something passes between them, a light flicker, almost a spark, and Bell sees Yue's face change. It goes slack, then bright, then puzzled, like a woman hearing a strain of music from a far-off room. Her free hand rises to her ear. Her lips part.

"Oh," she says aloud, in a thin cracked voice that has not spoken in decades. "Oh."

Mo Yan smiles.

She says nothing. She never does. But she lifts the charcoal in her other hand and draws a small neat circle on the wall above the cot, and then, beneath it, a line, and Yue reads it as she has read a thousand signs. A bell. A bell, and a bird.

"I hear it," says Yue. She is crying. "I hear the stair. I hear the kettle. I hear you." She laughs, sobbing. "You are humming. Did you know? You hum all the time, little one. You've been humming since I came in."

A thread of blood runs from Mo Yan's left nostril. She does not notice. Or she notices, and does not mind. She wipes it on her sleeve with the neat unconcern of a child blotting ink.

"Stop," says Bell, stepping forward. "She's bleeding. It costs her..."

It's fair, the charcoal says, on the wall. It's a small price.

Bell stops.

She looks at the old deaf woman, weeping, with her hand locked in the child's. She looks at the thread of red, and the girl's untroubled face. She thinks, I am a healer. I am supposed to prevent this. And she thinks, I do not have the right.

"Ten minutes," she says. "Then I'm giving her a handkerchief."

* * *

Qinghe finds them at dawn, and the whole thing turns inside out.

Bell is not there when it begins. She has gone to the washroom to scrub her hands, and when she comes back, the infirmary door is open and the room is full of steam. Qinghe stands at the center of it, in her blue smock, with the black kettle on one hip and a great steaming cauldron borne in by two scullions. Her white hair is bound under a wet cloth. Her face is flushed, and fierce, and very kind.

She is looking at the seven children as if she has been waiting for them all her life.

"Sit," she says. "All of you. At the table."

There is no table. She has had one carried in: the long oak one from the Great Kitchen, scarred, ink-stained, built to seat twenty. It stands under the windows in the early light, laid with seven wooden bowls and seven horn spoons. Seven stools. One for each. And on the end, a little apart, an eighth: tall-backed, worn, with a blue cushion.

The children look at it. Nobody moves.

"I don't understand," says Cheng Hui slowly.

"It is breakfast," says Qinghe.

"But we..."

"You are Jian's brothers. That makes you mine." She sets the kettle on the table with a thump. "I have been told you are fading. I have been told the Hall's thread will fray and you will go quiet and sleepy, and I am a cook, not a healer, so I do not claim to understand it. But I know one thing. A child who is fed at a table belongs to the table."

Silence.

"That isn't medicine," says Bell, from the doorway. Her voice is hoarse. "Qinghe, it can't..."

"Can't it?" Qinghe turns. Her eyes are bright. "I formed a Core eleven days ago. A hearth. It feeds on appetite and gives it back as healing. Your own Jian told me so, with his Scan. I do not know how far it reaches. But I know it has never once failed a hungry child." She lifts the ladle. "I propose to find out."

Bell opens her mouth. She finds there is nothing to say.

Tao is the first. He clambers up on a stool, kicking his heels, and holds out his bowl with both hands. Qinghe ladles. The broth steams gold. He sips, and his eyes go round, and he laughs aloud.

"It's warm," he says. "It's warm inside."

"Eat it all."

"I will!"

One by one the others follow. Cheng Hui first, stiffly, then Zhen Li, then Hai Ren, then the girl Mo Yan, who tastes hers and goes very still. Duan Ke is last. He stands for a long moment with the bowl in his hands, scowling, and Qinghe waits. She does not hurry him. She holds the ladle and the kettle and lets him come to it in his own time. At last, with a short sullen jerk of the head, he sits.

"I don't like soup," he says.

"I know."

"It's probably going to be disgusting."

"Probably."

He drinks. His eyes close.

Bell watches. She cannot not watch. She has come forward without meaning to, to stand at the foot of the table, and she lays her fingers lightly on Tao's wrist, and counts. She feels the thread. It is fraying. It is thin as a hair. She waits.

A minute passes. Then two.

And under her fingers, slowly, almost imperceptibly, the silver tension thickens.

It is no more than a flicker. A tightening. A single strand, among thousands, drawing taut. But it is there. She feels it as one feels a pulse come back in a limb that has gone numb: a prickle, a warmth, a tiny insistent yes. She opens her eyes. Tao is looking up at her, cheeks bulging, spoon in his fist, with an expression of intense satisfaction.

"I'm getting stronger," he says.

"Yes," whispers Bell. "I think you are."

She turns. Qinghe is watching her, across the steaming cauldron. The old woman's face is white and set and entirely calm.

"It will cost something," says Bell. Her throat is tight. "It always does."

"I know."

"Every day. For the rest of their lives. You won't be able to leave this kitchen for more than a night."

"I have not left it in a hundred years." Qinghe smiles. It is a small, crooked, tender smile. "I shall need a bigger kettle."

Bell sits down. She does it quite suddenly, on the nearest stool, with her hands over her face. She does not know whether she is laughing or weeping. It makes no difference. The children are eating. Tao is demanding a second bowl. And somewhere behind her, in the doorway, a thin gray man in a blanket has appeared and is standing very still, with one hand on the frame, looking at a table he has waited his whole life to see.
